props.title: Revolutionary Road
props.initialSlug: A couple's suburban dreams unravel into despair

sections.content: Revolutionary Road reunites Kate Winslet and Leonardo DiCaprio in a devastating portrait of 1950s suburban despair. Unlike their romantic pairing in Titanic (1997), here they capture the slow-burning destruction of a marriage with unflinching rawness. Director Sam Mendes builds on his exploration of suburban malaise from American Beauty (1999), but strips away the satirical elements for a more intimate psychological drama. The film adaptation of Richard Yates' novel expertly captures the suffocating conformity of post-war America, where dreams of European escape and artistic fulfillment crash against the beige walls of Connecticut domesticity.

sections.content: The suburban dream turned nightmare became a powerful theme in American cinema, particularly reflecting the disillusionment of the post-war era. The Ice Storm (1997) examines similar territory through the lens of the early 1970s, while American Beauty (1999) updates the critique for the pre-millennial period. These films share DNA with earlier works like The Graduate (1967), all questioning the hollow promise of material success and social conformity.

The performances in Revolutionary Road tap into a rich tradition of domestic drama, recalling the intensity of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1966) and the psychological complexity of Scenes from a Marriage (1973). Michael Shannon's supporting role as John Givings provides a crucial outsider perspective, his mental illness paradoxically making him the most clear-sighted character about the couple's self-deception. SUBHEAD: Marriage and Disillusionment in Modern Cinema

movies.title: Kramer vs. Kramer
movies.slug: Dustin Hoffman and Meryl Streep deliver powerful performances in this groundbreaking divorce drama

sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in later explorations of marital discord like Blue Valentine (2010) and Marriage Story (2019). These contemporary works share Revolutionary Road's unflinching examination of how dreams and reality collide within relationships, though they drop the period setting for modern contexts. The technical precision of Roger Deakins' cinematography in Revolutionary Road creates a visual prison of perfect homes and manicured lawns, influencing later films like Little Children (2006) and Carol (2015) in their portrayal of suffocating suburban environments.
